clinicalPearls: Sudden headache precipitated by coughing, sneezing or other Valsalva manoeuvres, not by sustained physical exertion
Pain is typically bilateral and posterior, lasting seconds to a few minutes
It occurs mainly in older adults, in contrast to the younger age of primary exercise headache
A Chiari type I malformation or other posterior fossa lesion is the key secondary cause to exclude
Brain imaging with attention to the craniocervical junction is recommended in most cases
The primary form often responds to indometacin
reference.pathophysiology: Primary cough headache is attributed to a transient rise in intracranial pressure and venous distension provoked by the Valsalva manoeuvre, in the absence of a structural lesion. The same mechanical stress can unmask symptomatic cough headache when there is crowding at the foramen magnum, as in Chiari malformation, or a posterior fossa mass, which is why exclusion of these is essential before accepting a primary diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior fossa tumour or other mass lesion
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain including the craniocervical junction
Neurological examination for posterior fossa or long-tract signs
History clarifying Valsalva versus sustained-exertion triggers
Further vascular imaging if a secondary vascular cause is suspected
redFlags: Cerebellar or brainstem signs on examination
Occipital pain with features of tonsillar descent
First or worst headache suggesting a vascular event
reference.prognosis: The primary form is benign and may remit over months to a few years; prognosis of symptomatic cough headache depends on the underlying structural cause.
pitfalls: Diagnosing primary cough headache without imaging and missing a Chiari malformation
Confusing it with primary exercise headache
Overlooking a thunderclap presentation that needs urgent vascular workup
Assuming benignity in a young patient without exclusion of structural disease
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Offer indometacin as first-line symptomatic and preventive treatment
Exclude a Chiari type I malformation or posterior fossa lesion with craniocervical-junction MRI before accepting the primary diagnosis
Treat any underlying chronic cough or respiratory condition to reduce the Valsalva trigger
Consider alternative preventives such as acetazolamide or topiramate if indometacin is not tolerated
Reassure the patient about the benign, often self-limiting course
Refer to neurology if features are atypical or a secondary cause is suspected
